title: Influence of reorientation angle and interlayer time on the microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties of 316L stainless steel fabricated by WAAM
abstract: Abstract Wire and Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) has emerged as an efficient technology for producing large-scale metallic components, achieving up to 90% energy efficiency compared with powder-based laser or electron-beam processes. However, the relationship between deposition parameters and the final quality of WAAM parts remains not fully understood, particularly regarding microstructural anisotropy, mechanical performance, and corrosion resistance. The principal contribution of this study lies in the integrated processing framework adopted, which combines bead-geometry optimisation, inter-bead spacing optimisation, precise control of the interlayer dwell time (ILDT), and the implementation of 0°, 67°, and 90° interlayer reorientation strategies, enabling the correlation of crystallographic texture with mechanical behavior and corrosion response evaluated in three directions in WAAM-fabricated 316L stainless steel. Optimal deposition parameters were defined, and samples were analyzed using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), mechanical testing, and electrochemical corrosion measurements. The results showed that higher welding speeds increased the bead aspect ratio, while higher wire feed rates reduced it, also influencing the contact angle, which decreased as the deposition rate increased. Shorter interlayer intervals reduced total fabrication time but affected surface flatness and finish, depending on the reorientation angle. Mechanically, specimens produced with 67° and 90° reorientation angles exhibited reduced grain orientation, higher strength, and more homogeneous austenitic microstructures with a lower ferrite fraction. Regarding corrosion behavior, samples fabricated with a 67° reorientation angle in the TWD direction showed more positive corrosion potential and enhanced passivation capacity, indicating improved stability in aggressive environments. Overall, the results highlight the critical role of precise control of reorientation angle and interlayer time in balancing productivity, mechanical integrity, and corrosion resistance in WAAM-fabricated components. The findings reinforce the potential of process optimization to expand WAAM’s industrial applicability, particularly in marine, oil and gas, automotive, and power generation sectors, where components require high strength and corrosion resistance. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) has emerged as a promising route for producing large-scale metallic components due to its high deposition rate, low material cost, and high productivity compared with powder-based additive manufacturing processes [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4 ]. Among candidate alloys, stainless steels are particularly attractive because of their weldability, mechanical performance, and corrosion resistance [ 5 ,  6 ]. However, the layer-by-layer nature of WAAM imposes repeated thermal cycles, heat accumulation, and directional solidification, which strongly influence microstructural evolution and, consequently, the final properties of the deposited material [ 3 ,  7 ,  8 ,  9 ,  10 – 11 ].

In WAAM, the quality and reliability of fabricated components are governed by the cumulative thermal history developed during multilayer deposition, rather than by the nominal heat input of a single pass. Successive layers repeatedly reheat previously solidified material, generating heating–cooling cycles, progressive heat accumulation, and spatially non-uniform thermal gradients. Gupta and Mulik [ 12 ,  13 ] showed that these gradients increase with build height as heat conduction toward the substrate becomes less effective, with the average thermal gradient rising from 1.525 °C/mm after the first layer to 24.78 °C/mm after the fourth layer. Such gradients directly affect solidification behavior, grain morphology, crystallographic texture, residual stress development, dimensional stability, and mechanical-property uniformity. Moreover, recent thermo-mechanical analyses have shown that the highest tensile residual stresses concentrate at the substrate–wall interface and lower root corners, reaching 226 MPa on the top surface and 282 MPa at the substrate–wall corner, where severe thermal gradients and geometric mismatch coexist. Therefore, controlling heat accumulation and repeated thermal cycling is essential to mitigate distortion, cracking susceptibility, anisotropy, and loss of structural integrity in WAAM-fabricated components.

One of the main consequences of these thermal conditions is the development of epitaxial growth, columnar grains, and crystallographic texture, which may lead to anisotropic mechanical behavior in WAAM-fabricated stainless steels [ 4 ]. Previous studies have shown that austenitic stainless steel components produced by WAAM can exhibit directional variations in yield strength, ductility, and elastic–plastic response as a result of preferential grain orientation and build-direction-aligned columnar microstructures [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ]. Therefore, controlling the thermal history during deposition is essential to reduce microstructural anisotropy and improve the consistency of mechanical performance.

Among the process variables that govern thermal history, interlayer dwell time (ILDT) plays a critical role because it directly affects heat accumulation, cooling rate, remelting, and grain growth. In WAAM-fabricated stainless steels, increasing ILDT has been associated with lower interpass temperatures, microstructural refinement, and changes in hardness, strength, and corrosion behavior, although excessively short or long dwell times may be detrimental [ 17 ,  18 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 – 22 ]. Likewise, in other WAAM alloys, ILDT has also been linked to reductions in grain size and crystallographic texture intensity [ 23 ,  24 ]. These findings indicate that ILDT is a relevant parameter for tailoring both microstructure and properties.

Another strategy for modifying thermal gradients and solidification conditions is the rotation of the deposition path between successive layers. This approach has been widely studied in laser-based additive manufacturing, where interlayer rotation has been shown to alter texture development, grain morphology, residual stress distribution, and anisotropy [ 25 ,  26 ,  27 ,  28 ,  29 ,  30 ,  31 – 32 ]. In particular, rotation angles near 67° have often been associated with more homogeneous thermal redistribution and reduced preferential grain alignment compared with 90° strategies [ 33 ,  34 ,  35 – 36 ]. Despite these advances, the combined effect of ILDT and interlayer reorientation on directional texture, mechanical behavior, and corrosion performance remains insufficiently explored in arc-based processes such as WAAM, especially for stainless steels [ 37 ,  38 ,  39 ,  40 ,  41 – 42 ].

Recent studies on arc-based additive manufacturing processes have demonstrated that the deposition strategy has a significant influence on the behavior of 316L stainless steel components. In WAAM, zigzag and hybrid deposition strategies with 45° and 90° reorientations have been associated with changes in mechanical response and corrosion behavior. Similarly, in DED-Arc, different deposition strategies have been related to variations in microstructure, crystallographic texture, hardness, mechanical properties, and residual stresses. These studies have established the deposition path as an important variable for microstructural and functional control [ 43 ,  44 ]. However, it remains insufficiently understood how bead geometry, inter-bead spacing, interlayer dwell time, and interlayer reorientation act jointly on the evolution of directional texture, mechanical anisotropy, and corrosion response in WAAM-fabricated 316L components. This gap is particularly relevant because previous directional assessments were limited to two principal directions, whereas the mechanical response of multilayer components may depend on additional orientations associated with the build direction and deposition path.

In this context, the present study investigates the WAAM processing of 316L stainless steel through an integrated processing route combining preliminary bead-geometry parameterization, inter-bead spacing selection, two interlayer dwell times, 2 and 5 min, and three reorientation angles, 0°, 67°, and 90°, applied through a zigzag deposition strategy [ 45 ]. The selection of 316L stainless steel is particularly relevant because of its widespread structural use and its favorable combination of weldability, mechanical strength, and corrosion resistance [ 46 ,  47 ]. The central contribution of this study is to demonstrate how the coupled control of ILDT and interlayer reorientation, especially the 67° strategy, modifies the thermal history, disrupts the continuity of columnar growth, weakens preferential texture development, and affects mechanical anisotropy evaluated in three directions, as well as global corrosion resistance. In this way, this work aims to establish a more direct relationship between processing strategy, microstructural evolution, and functional performance in WAAM-fabricated 316L stainless steel components.

sections.heading: 316L wire and base metal
paragraphs: In the WAAM process, a commercial stainless-steel wire supplied as 316L, with a diameter of 1.2 mm and provided by WELDCENTER, was used as the feedstock material. Several 1020 carbon steel plates were employed as substrate material. The chemical composition of the as-received wire feedstock, expressed in weight percent (wt%), is presented in Table  1 . The concentrations of Cr, Cu, Fe, Mn, Mo, Ni, P, and Si were determined by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) using an iCAP6500 instrument manufactured by Thermo Scientific, following the SMWW 3120 B methodology after complete digestion in aqua regia. The C and S contents were determined by combustion and quantified via infrared absorption using a LECO CS-844 analyser, in accordance with ASTM E1019-18 [ 48 ]. sections.heading: WAAM component fabrication system
paragraphs: The components investigated in this study were manufactured using the WAAM process in a laboratory-scale research facility under controlled experimental conditions. A schematic representation of the WAAM system employed in the present study is provided in Fig.  1 .  Deposition was carried out using a Pulsarc 6200 Max welding power source (Eutectic Castolin) operating in constant-voltage mode, coupled with an integrated CNC system to control the movement of the deposition torch along three axes, which was operated through Mach3 software. Process parameters, including travel speed and deposition trajectory, were defined to ensure adequate geometric and dimensional control of the fabricated components and were experimentally calibrated prior to deposition to ensure repeatability of the manufacturing conditions. A prior calibration of the wire feeding system was performed. Although the welding equipment provides controlled wire feeding, the system used in this study indicates the wire feed setting through the regulator position rather than directly displaying the feed rate in mm/min. Therefore, the actual wire feed speed was experimentally determined by measuring the length of wire delivered over a 10 s interval. This procedure enabled the correlation between regulator positions and the corresponding wire feed rate to be established, allowing accurate process parameterization and ensuring stable WAAM deposition conditions. Fig. 1 Schematic diagram of the Experimental WAAM system employed in the present work

sections.heading: Determination of the optimal deposition bead parameters
paragraphs: The procedure undertaken to determine the optimal operating parameters and establish the most appropriate configuration for the fabrication of cubic parts in the WAAM process, as well as to evaluate their influence on the quality of the deposition beads, is outlined below.

sections.heading: Definition of factors and responses
paragraphs: In the initial stage, the process parameters that would remain constant, as well as those that would be varied during the deposition of single beads on the substrate, were established. The fixed parameters utilized in the experiment, and their corresponding values are detailed in Table  2 . The variable factors considered in the factorial design were the welding speed (Vs) and the wire feeding speed (WFS). The study was conducted based on a three-level, two-factor factorial design, as presented in Table  3 . The values of the independent variables were determined from literature data, experimental results obtained in preliminary tests, and recommendations provided by the wire manufacturer. For each possible combination of factors and their respective levels, three experimental replications were performed, resulting in a total of 27 measurements taken from the deposited beads. The response variables evaluated in this study were the heat input, the aspect ratio, and the contact angle, which are fundamental parameters for the geometric and energetic characterization of the WAAM process. sections.heading: Deposition of beads and acquisition of response variables
Fabrication of parallelepiped specimens
paragraphs: To determine the appropriate distance between adjacent deposition beads, four parallelepiped specimens (P00-W6, P00-W7, P90-W6, and P90-W7) were fabricated. All samples were produced with a 2-min interlayer cooling time on AISI 1020 carbon steel plates measuring 150 mm × 100 mm × 8 mm. The specimens were manufactured using the bead parameters selected in Phase I of the methodology, following a zigzag deposition strategy. Each parallelepiped consisted of four deposited layers, resulting in a uniform final height. On one base, four parallel deposition tracks were deposited, while the opposite side had a length of 50 ± 4 mm. The center-to-center distances between adjacent beads were defined based on values commonly adopted in the literature for WAAM processes, from which two representative spacings were selected for experimental evaluation [ 50 ,  51 – 52 ]. Table  4  summarizes the center-to-center distances between adjacent beads (where  W  represents the bead width) and the reorientation angles applied during the fabrication of the parallelepiped specimens. sections.heading: Fabrication of blocks
paragraphs: Six block specimens with approximate dimensions of 60 × 60 × 35 mm were fabricated, each consisting of eighteen deposited layers using a zigzag deposition strategy. During the process, different interlayer dwell times and reorientation angles were applied, as detailed in Table  4 . The substrate material consisted of AISI 1020 carbon steel plates measuring 240 × 150 mm with a thickness of 8 mm. The fabrication of each block required individual programming of every layer in the CNC control system. Figure  2  illustrates the sequence of deposited layers, highlighting the geometric arrangement and build strategy adopted during the process. The layers were deposited along the building direction (BD) until completing a total of 18 layers for each fabricated sample. For reorientation angles of 0° and 90°, four main layers were repeated cyclically until the final height was achieved. In the case of the 67° reorientation angle, each layer was individually programmed, following a specific toolpath designed for that orientation. Fig. 2 Three-dimensional representation of the layer-by-layer deposition paths at different reorientation angles adopted in the WAAM process:  a  0°,  b  90°, and  c  67°. Each color represents a distinct layer, while the symbols indicate the start point (blue sphere) and the end point (red cone) of each deposition trajectory

sections.heading: Microstructural and chemical characterization
paragraphs: For the microstructural and Chemical characterization, a Thermo Fisher Scientific Quanta 650 FEG scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with a Schottky field-emission gun (FEG) was used. This instrument was employed to perform linear chemical analyses via EDX and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analyses. The EBSD data was processed using the ATEX software. The samples for these analyses were extracted from each WAAM-fabricated block by electrical discharge machining (EDM) to ensure dimensional precision and preservation of microstructural integrity. The specimens were standardized to 1 cm × 1 cm in area and 2 mm in depth, as shown in Fig.  3 a. Fig. 3 Schematic representations of the sampling and analysis procedures conducted in this study:  a  Extraction scheme of the samples from the WAAM-fabricated blocks, showing the dimensions and the analysis directions for EBSD: AWD (Advance Welding Direction), TWD (Transversal Welding Direction), and BD (Build Direction);  b  CAD schematic representation of the orientations analyzed for the mechanical anisotropy evaluation in the WAAM process;  c  Miniature tensile specimen used in the mechanical tests;  d  CAD scheme of the analyzed directions for electrochemical tests

The coordinate system used to orient all the analyses was defined based on the geometric configuration of the WAAM process: TWD (Transversal Welding Direction)—parallel to the alignment of the deposition beads, taking the first layer as reference, BD (Build Direction)—corresponding to the stacking direction of successive layers and AWD (Advance Welding Direction)—representing the longitudinal or travel direction of the deposition beads with respect to the first fabricated layer. Analyses were conducted considering the X-axis as BD, the Y-axis as TWD (perpendicular to BD), and the Z-axis aligned with the AWD direction. Based on this reference system, linear EDS chemical analysis, with a scan length of 500 μm, was performed in the central region of each sample, corresponding to the plane between the TWD and BD directions. The line scan encompassed all points along its trajectory, including grains, grain boundaries, and regions of higher contrast observed in the micrographs, enabling the acquisition of elemental distribution profiles that revealed compositional variations among the analyzed elements.

During EBSD data acquisition, the samples were tilted by 70° relative to the horizontal plane. Each of the six samples was mounted in cylindrical holders and positioned in the EBSD device. The operating parameters included an acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a spot size of 5.0, and an objective aperture of 1000 µm. The analysis encompassed three distinct regions of each block (top, middle, and bottom), enabling the investigation of microstructural and structural characteristics at different building heights. In each region, an area of 4 mm 2  was examined, with adjacent areas combined to perform a global analysis covering a larger number of grains and thereby enhancing statistical representativeness. This approach enabled a comprehensive assessment of the crystalline phases, grain morphology, and crystallographic texture. For texture analysis, Inverted Pole Figures (IPFs) were calculated, providing a detailed representation of the preferred crystal orientations. The collected crystallographic orientations were combined to compute the Orientation Distribution Function (ODF), allowing a continuous representation of crystal orientations and describing the overall texture in the TWD–BD plane. Furthermore, smaller and specific subregions within the main areas were analyzed to obtain local information about the crystalline phases present. This combination of global and localized analyses provided a comprehensive understanding of the microstructural characteristics of the blocks fabricated by the WAAM process.

sections.heading: Mechanical characterization and corrosion studies
paragraphs: The parts fabricated by the WAAM process may exhibit anisotropic mechanical behavior due to the intrinsic characteristics of the layer-by-layer deposition process. To investigate this anisotropy, tensile specimens were extracted from the WAAM-fabricated blocks. Tensile tests were performed in three specific orientations, designated as AWD (Advance Welding Direction), DD (Diagonal Direction), and TWD (Transversal Welding Direction), all defined with respect to the first deposited layer, as illustrated in Fig.  3 b. These orientations correspond to analysis angles of 0°, 45° and 90° relative to the deposition direction. Considering the dimensional limitations of the blocks, miniature tensile specimens were machined. Most of their dimensions followed those reported by Zhang [ 53 ], with minor modifications introduced to adapt the samples to the testing apparatus, as shown in Fig.  3 c.

A total of 36 tensile tests were conducted. Each test involved the application of a uniaxial load until fracture, with the testing system properly calibrated for this purpose. The results enabled the evaluation of mechanical properties, including ultimate tensile strength (UTS), elongation, and Young’s modulus, for each orientation analyzed. To statistically compare the mechanical properties among the different orientations, an analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a Tukey post-hoc test was performed at a 95% confidence level. This approach allowed the identification of statistically significant differences in the mechanical behavior across the directions studied, providing a comprehensive understanding of the anisotropy of the material produced by the WAAM process.

To evaluate the influence of different manufacturing conditions, such as interlayer dwell time, reorientation angle, and the TWD, AWD, and BD directions on the corrosion performance in an aggressive medium, samples obtained from 316L stainless steel blocks fabricated by the WAAM process with a total surface area of 1 cm 2  were extracted along each of these orientations, as illustrated in Fig.  3 d. Each sample underwent meticulous metallographic preparation, which involved progressive grinding with abrasive papers of 800, 1200, 2500, and 4000 mesh. This was followed by polishing using cloths impregnated with polycrystalline diamond pastes of 6, 3, 1, and 0.25 µm. This comprehensive procedure ensured that the surfaces were uniform and free of defects, making them suitable for subsequent electrochemical testing. In the present study two types of electrochemical tests were employed: open circuit potential (OCP) and potentiodynamic polarization tests. The electrochemical tests were carried out by using an electrochemical cell containing a compartment of three electrodes: working electrode (WE) of 316L stainless steel with an exposed area of approximately 0.19 cm 2 , counter electrode (CE) of platinum, and saturated calomel (Hg/Hg₂Cl₂, KCl sat ) as reference electrode. All the electrochemical tests were performed by using a μStat-i-400 s potentiostat/galvanostat (Bi). Corrosion tests were carried out in a 0.6 mol L⁻ 1  NaCl aqueous solution under controlled laboratory conditions. The E ocp  was monitored during 1 h for each sample. The potentiodynamic polarization curves were recorded over a potential range of − 0.7 to 0.5 V/SCE, at a scan rate of 0.1 mV s⁻ 1 . All electrochemical measurements were performed in triplicate to ensure reproducibility and statistical reliability of the results. This methodology provided consistent and reproducible data regarding the corrosion behavior of the analyzed samples. Finally, the electrochemical parameters were determined by Tafel extrapolation using the DropView 8400 software.

sections.heading: Weld bead analysis and parameter selection for WAAM
paragraphs: Figure  4 a shows the top view of the WAAM-deposited beads. A visual inspection of the bead surface indicates the presence of metallic spatters generated during the deposition process. No clear evidence of surface porosity or silicate inclusions was identified in the observed regions. Table  5  and Fig.  4 b present the results of the profilometric analysis and the calculated heat input. The travel speed (Vs) strongly affects the stability of the molten pool. Although higher speeds increase productivity, they can also induce hydrodynamic instabilities, such as Kelvin–Helmholtz and Plateau–Rayleigh, which lead to geometrical discontinuities and the humping phenomenon [ 54 ,  55 ,  56 – 57 ]. This occurs because the molten pool elongates and loses stability, fragmenting into smaller droplets to restore capillary pressure equilibrium. Despite these potential issues, the beads produced in this study exhibited a uniform and stable deposition, without significant geometrical defects. However, variations in the amount of spatter were observed, being more pronounced at Vs = 600 mm/min and WFS = 4400 mm/min, Vs = 500 mm/min and WFS = 5520 mm/min, and Vs = 500 mm/min and WFS = 7020 mm/min. This increase in spatter formation is likely associated with the higher wire feed rate and localized rise in arc energy, which affect the stability of the molten pool and the surface morphology of the deposited material Fig. 4 Deposition beads obtained under different welding speed (Vs) and wire feed speed (WFS) conditions:  a  top-view images of the deposited weld beads for the evaluated Vs and WFS combinations;  b  corresponding deposited beads and their cross-sectional profiles, illustrating the influence of Vs and WFS on bead geometry and penetration characteristics Table 5 Values of the independent and dependent variables used in the experiments Velocity speed (mm/min) Wire feed speed (mm/min) Voltage (V) Current (A) Average heat input (J/mm) Average aspect ratio (mm/mm) Average contact angle (°) 400 4440 19.2 156 359.42 2.35 137.45 400 5520 19.2 180 414.72 1.94 122.74 400 7020 18.4 192 423.94 1.97 112.29 500 4440 19.2 156 287.54 2.45 142.59 500 5520 19.2 180 331.78 2.26 129.96 500 7020 18 204 352.51 1.94 111.35 600 4440 19.2 156 239.62 2.62 142.65 600 5520 19.2 180 276.48 2.45 129.35 600 7020 18.0 204 293.76 1.99 115.14

According to this model, the Vs parameter directly affects the aspect ratio. As Vs increases, the bead height decreases due to the reduced material deposition resulting from faster torch movement. This reduction leads to an increase in aspect ratio, showing a positive correlation between Vs and aspect ratio, while bead height is inversely related. Kannan and Yoganandh [ 57 ] reported a similar trend, in which bead width and height increased with wire feed rate but decreased as welding speed rose. Consistently, the model developed in this study indicates that higher WFS values result in greater material deposition, leading to increased bead height and, consequently, a reduction in aspect ratio. The negative coefficient associated with WFS confirms this inverse relationship, highlighting its strong influence on bead geometry.

The optimal parameters defined for the fabrication of the solid samples by WAAM were Vs = 600 mm/min and WFS = 5520 mm/min. The corresponding cross-sectional profile exhibits a parabolic shape, resulting from the relationship between wire feed speed and welding speed, which yielded a ratio of 9.2. When this ratio is below 12.5, a parabolic cross-sectional profile is typically observed [ 58 ]. This behavior was confirmed by profilometry analyses (see Figs.  5 a) of the samples produced under these conditions. The selection of this Vs–WFS combination was motivated by its high average aspect ratio (2.45), where the bead width exceeds its height, thus promoting layer overlap with reduced spatter formation. The selection of this aspect ratio is further supported by its alignment with the optimal range reported in the literature for WAAM processes, typically between 2 and 3, where a balance between geometric control, process stability, and defect mitigation is achieved [ 59 ,  60 – 61 ]. In this context, the width-to-height relationship governs inter-track spacing and layer height, directly influencing dimensional accuracy and build consistency [ 62 ,  63 ]. From a metallurgical perspective, maintaining an appropriate aspect ratio is essential to ensure effective interlayer coalescence, minimizing defects such as lack of fusion and promoting the structural integrity of the deposited material [ 64 ]. Furthermore, higher values within this optimal range have been associated with improved surface uniformity and reduced waviness, facilitating subsequent layer deposition and enhancing build homogeneity [ 65 ,  66 – 67 ]. Additionally, this geometric configuration promotes near-net-shape deposition, reducing the need for post-processing and improving material utilization efficiency [ 65 ]. Fig. 5 Contour plots and three-dimensional visualization . a  3D view of the weld bead corresponding to the selected condition (Vs = 600 mm/min and WFS = 5520 mm/min).  b  Aspect ratio variation as a function of welding speed (Vs) and wire feed speed (WFS),  c  Heat input variation as a function of Vs and WFS

In contrast, the configuration of 600 mm/min and 4400 mm/min, although exhibiting a slightly higher aspect ratio (2.65), showed increased spatter during visual inspection. Furthermore, the 600–5520 mm/min condition exhibited the second-lowest heat input among all tested setups, contributing to lower thermal variation during successive deposition cycles. The selection of relatively low heat input conditions is consistent with their reported influence on microstructural refinement and process stability, as reduced heat input promotes more homogeneous microstructures and more uniform properties along the build height [ 38 ,  68 ,  69 – 70 ]. In addition, lower heat input has been associated with improved corrosion resistance in stainless steels due to reduced elemental segregation and a more uniform distribution of alloying elements such as Cr and Mo, which are critical for passive film stability [ 38 ,  71 ]. Furthermore, reduced heat input contributes to improved surface quality and a lower tendency for defect formation, enhancing the overall stability and reliability of WAAM deposition [ 70 ,  72 ].

These relationships are illustrated in the contour plots shown in Figs.  5 b and c, which represent the variation of aspect ratio and heat input, respectively, as a function of the welding parameters. It can be observed that the Vs = 600 mm/min and WFS = 5520 mm/min condition lies within a region of low heat input and a balanced aspect ratio, confirming its suitability for stable and homogeneous material deposition. Finally, all analyzed beads presented contact angles above 90°, which did not significantly affect parameter selection. It is also noteworthy that this configuration showed no undercuts, and the reinforcement remained free of surface porosity.

sections.heading: Selection of the optimal inter-bead distance for WAAM-fabricated blocks
paragraphs: The parallelepipeds fabricated with reorientation angles of 0° and 90° and two different center-to-center distances exhibited variations in final geometry and surface quality, as shown in Fig.  6 a–f and g–l. In general, the condition employing 0.667 × W was associated with taller parallelepipeds and improved geometric regularity, as well as a tendency toward reduced lateral waviness, although differences in surface finish among the conditions were moderate. For the 0° configuration, comparison between P00-W6 and P00-W7 indicated an approximate 8.5% reduction in height when 0.738 × W was used, accompanied by increased lateral irregularity in the transverse sections. A similar trend was observed for 90°, with P90-W6 exhibiting a height approximately 7.5% greater than that of P90-W7, together with slightly more continuous lateral profiles. Overall, these results indicate that both the reorientation angle and the center-to-center distance influence the geometry and surface quality of the deposited structures, with 0.667 × W representing the most favorable condition by enabling greater height per fabrication unit and, consequently, improved process productivity, dimensional stability, and facilitation of subsequent layer deposition, without a significant detriment to surface finish. For this reason, this distance was selected for the subsequent stages of the study; considering W = 6.0081425 mm, the adopted center-to-center distance was approximately 4.01 mm. Fig. 6 Macrophotographs of the cross-sections and diagonal and top views of the parallelepipeds fabricated with different reorientation angles and center-to-center distances:  a – c  P00-W6,  d – f  P00-W7,  g – i  P90-W6, and  j – l  P90-W7

Figure  7  presents images of the WAAM blocks fabricated with interlayer dwell times of 2 and 5 min under reorientation angles of 0°, 67°, and 90°. The blocks manufactured with a 0° reorientation angle, shown in Fig.  7 a–d ,  exhibited reduced flatness on both the top and lateral surfaces, leading to pronounced geometric irregularities, particularly in the upper region. The blocks produced with a 67° reorientation angle, displayed in Figs.  7 e–h, showed an intermediate behavior, with good flatness and surface quality on the top surface, while lower homogeneity was observed on the lateral surfaces due to the greater geometric complexity associated with this deposition strategy. In contrast, the blocks fabricated with a 90° reorientation angle, illustrated in Figs.  7 i–l demonstrated the best overall performance in terms of surface finish and geometric uniformity, exhibiting improved flatness on both the top and lateral surfaces. The observed variations in flatness and uniformity, more pronounced in the upper regions of the blocks, can be attributed to differences in thermal input associated with each reorientation angle, as well as to the influence of interlayer dwell time on molten pool stability and solidification behavior. Higher thermal input increased the temperature of the substrate or previously deposited layer, hindering heat dissipation and compromising control over the deposited layer height, ultimately resulting in variations in surface uniformity [ 73 ]. Fig. 7 WAAM-fabricated blocks shown in front and diagonal views.  a – b  C2-00;  c – d  C5-00;  e – f  C2-67;  g – h  C5-67;  i – j  C2-90;  k – l  C5-90

The total fabrication time showed a significant reduction as the interlayer time decreased. Blocks produced a 5-min interlayer time required, on average, 2 h and 6 min, whereas those manufactured with 2 min were completed in 1 h and 10 min, representing a 44.4% reduction in total fabrication time. This variation highlighted the influence of interlayer time on process efficiency; however, adjustments to this parameter may affect the quality and final properties of the material, requiring complementary analyses. Although the block height after the deposition of 18 layers was similar regardless of interlayer time, the lateral surfaces of all samples displayed the characteristic waviness of the layer-by-layer process. These irregularities can be removed through additional finishing, such as machining, to achieve a more uniform surface.

sections.heading: Linear EDS chemical profiling of All WAAM-fabricated blocks
paragraphs: The linear EDS analysis was performed to evaluate compositional variations along the deposited tracks, with particular emphasis on identifying chemical heterogeneities associated with non-metallic inclusions. The results revealed noticeable compositional fluctuations among the analyzed samples, as shown in Fig.  8 a–f. In the C2-00 sample Fig.  8 a, a local increase in Mo signal intensity was observed along the scan line. With respect to the major elements, Fe exhibited relative reductions in peak intensity in samples C5-00 (Fig.  8 b), C2-67 (Fig.  8 c), and C5-90 (Fig.  8 f), indicating local variations in its relative weight fraction along the analyzed trajectories. When comparing the processing conditions, samples fabricated with an interlayer dwell time of 2 min (Fig.  8 a, c, and e) tended to exhibit slightly more homogeneous compositional behavior compared to those produced with a 5 min dwell time. All analyzed conditions showed a relative increase in Si content, more pronounced in C5-00, C2-67, and C5-90, accompanied by a more evident enrichment of Mn. Variations in oxygen content were more noticeable in C2-67, whereas C5-90 exhibited fewer localized fluctuations. In regions of higher contrast, the concurrent enrichment of Si, Mn, and O observed suggests the presence of non-metallic inclusions whose composition is compatible with complex oxides and/or silicate-type phases. The coexistence of these species is consistent with literature reports on WAAM-fabricated austenitic stainless steels, in which the nature of the inclusions may vary depending on their size and the local solidification conditions [ 74 ,  75 ,  76 ,  77 – 78 ]. Fig. 8 Weight-percent (wt%) distribution profiles over 500 µm across the microstructure, obtained by linear EDS, for each chemical element under the following conditions:  a  C2-00;  b  C5-00;  c  C2-67;  d  C5-67;  e  C2-90;  f  C5-90

sections.heading: EBSD-based characterization of FCC and BCC phases in WAAM-fabricated blocks
paragraphs: In addition, this behavior is closely associated with the relatively long interlayer cooling time applied after each deposition step onto AISI 1020 carbon steel substrate plates. This dwell time promotes efficient heat extraction toward the substrate, resulting in an effectively high cooling rate after each deposition, which hinders ferrite growth during solidification and subsequent cooling. In parallel, the thermal cycles associated with subsequent deposited layers promote the instability of previously formed ferrite, favoring its transformation or dissolution. As a result, the fraction of ferrite retained in the final microstructure is significantly reduced.

The quantitative assessment of phase fractions further suggests that the deposition reorientation angle, in interaction with the interlayer dwell time, influences the relative distribution of ferrite and austenite phases within the analyzed regions. For the 0° condition, comparison between C2-00 (Fig.  10 a) and C5-00 (Fig.  10 b) indicates that increasing the interlayer dwell time from 2 to 5 min tended to promote a marked increase in the BCC fraction, on the order of ~ 95%, highlighting the sensitivity of this configuration to temporal parameters. This behavior indicates that interlayer dwell time can modify the thermal cycle experienced by the material, affecting phase stability and transformation kinetics. Fig. 10 High-resolution phase maps obtained by EBSD for the different processing conditions:  a  C2-00;  b  C5-00;  c  C2-67;  d  C5-67;  e  C2-90;  f  C5-90

For the 67° angle, a similar trend was observed, although with a lower magnitude. In contrast, for the 90° condition, comparison between C2-90 (Fig.  10 e) and C5-90 (Fig.  10 f) revealed an additional reduction in the BCC fraction of approximately ~ 27% with increasing interlayer dwell time. Overall, the transition from 0° to 67° and 90° was associated with a progressive reduction in the BCC fraction, accompanied by a relative increase in the FCC fraction. This effect was most pronounced at 90°, particularly for the C5-90 condition (Fig.  10 f), where a relative decrease in the BCC fraction of ~ 79% was observed when compared with C5-00 (Fig.  10 b), while maintaining a constant interlayer dwell time of 5 min. These results reinforce that variations in processing parameters modify the local thermal history, which governs phase transformation and explains the reduced amount of retained ferrite. Additionally, it is suggested that the scanning angles employed, as the parameter exhibiting the most pronounced influence on phase fraction variations, may be associated with modifications in the local thermal history, thereby contributing to the observed differences in the amount of retained ferrite.

Crystallographic texture plays a relevant role in determining the properties of additively manufactured components, which justifies its analysis in the WAAM-fabricated blocks [ 87 ]. Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) images, presented in Fig.  11 a–f, show crystallographic orientation maps in the BD–TWD plane, while Fig.  11 g presents the corresponding inverse pole figure map, in which the colors indicate the predominant crystallographic orientation within each grain. It was observed that the main axis of the columnar grains tended to align with the build direction (BD), although this alignment was not uniform, with grain growth occurring in multiple orientations and deviations that varied from layer to layer, indicating the continuity of crystal growth across successive depositions. This behavior was associated with the coincidence between the direction of maximum heat flow and one of the preferred growth directions (EGD), namely ⟨001⟩, which is characteristic of cubic crystal structures [ 74 ]. Nevertheless, the scanning pattern may induce deviations from the local maximum thermal gradient, affecting the solidification orientation, as reported for Directed Energy Deposition (DED) processes [ 80 ,  88 ,  89 ,  90 – 91 ]. Consequently, the resulting textures reflect a dynamic balance between preferred growth directions and heat flow paths within the melt pool. In addition, the columnar grains exhibited a curved morphology associated with the melt pool geometry [ 92 ,  93 – 94 ], whose depth controlled the remelting of the previously deposited layer; the presence of residual or partially solidified material promoted greater dispersion of crystallographic orientations, leading to weaker textures and reduced crystallographic uniformity. Fig. 11 Crystallographic orientation maps obtained by EBSD:  a  C2-00;  b  C5-00;  c  C2-67;  d  C5-67;  e  C2-90;  f  C5-90;  g  Corresponding inverse pole figure (IPF)

Sample C2-00 (Fig.  11 a) exhibited a higher dispersion of crystallographic orientations, indicating the development of a less defined texture, whereas sample C5-00 (Fig.  11 b) showed a more pronounced texture, evidenced by the predominance of green hues in the orientation maps, associated with a preferential ⟨101⟩ orientation. This observation suggests that increasing the interlayer dwell time favored texture strengthening for the 0° reorientation angle. For the 67° reorientation angle, samples C2-67 (Fig.  11 c) and C5-67 (Fig.  11 d) exhibited a high dispersion of grain orientations regardless of the interlayer dwell time, resulting in a weaker texture and a more isotropic structure. In the case of samples fabricated with a 90° reorientation angle, a distinct behavior was observed. Sample C2-90 (Fig.  11 e) presented regions dominated by blue and violet tones, suggesting the presence of grains oriented along the ⟨111⟩ direction, whereas sample C5-90 (Fig.  11 f) exhibited greater variability of crystallographic orientations throughout the microstructure, evidenced by a more heterogeneous chromatic distribution.

These findings are consistent with the study of Gupta and Mulik on WAAM-fabricated Inconel 825, where process parameters were shown to govern microstructural development by modifying heat input and the effective cooling conditions. Higher heat input, associated with higher current and lower torch speed, favored prolonged dendritic growth and coarser columnar microstructures, whereas controlled heat input, higher torch speed, and pulsed deposition promoted faster cooling, finer dendrites, and more equiaxed grains. In the present study, although ILDT and path reorientation are the main variables, the same mechanism applies: ILDT controls heat dissipation between layers, while path reorientation modifies the heat-flow direction and the continuity of epitaxial growth. Thus, the 0° strategy tends to preserve repetitive thermal trajectories and stronger texture development, whereas the 67° strategy disrupts the continuity of columnar growth, increases the dispersion of crystallographic orientations, and favors a more isotropic microstructure [ 95 ].

The deposition angle configuration plays a relevant role in defining crystallographic texture in additively manufactured materials. In Ti-6Al-4 V alloys processed by Powder Bed Fusion (PBF), it has been reported that a 90° reorientation promotes the modification of an originally dominant fibrous ⟨100⟩ texture [ 96 ]. Similarly, Brito et al. [ 43 ] demonstrated that, in the fabrication of austenitic stainless steel 316L components, a 90° reorientation angle led to the development of a more pronounced fibrous {001} component along the build direction when compared with a 45° reorientation. In the present study, it was observed that the 0° condition resulted in a more intense texture than the 67° condition, indicating that specific deposition angles influence the continuity of epitaxial growth and the evolution of crystallographic orientations during the WAAM process. In this context, the behavior observed for the 67° condition can be understood in terms of its effect on the evolution of the thermal field across successive layers. While the 0° strategy maintains a consistent heat flow direction, promoting continuous epitaxial growth and the formation of elongated columnar grains [ 97 ], and the 90° strategy introduces an orthogonal but periodic variation in the thermal gradient, still enabling the development of structured and anisotropic textures [ 98 ], the 67° condition suppresses the systematic repetition of the deposition direction, resulting in a highly non-periodic thermal history [ 99 ].

This lack of periodicity leads to continuous changes in the direction of heat flow, generating a progressive misalignment between the thermal gradient and the preferred growth directions ⟨001⟩. As a result, epitaxial growth is disrupted, promoting the nucleation of new grains and dendritic branching along non-dominant directions, which contributes to the fragmentation of the columnar structure and increased dispersion of crystallographic orientations [ 100 ]. Furthermore, the interaction between the 67° rotation and the melt pool geometry enhances the complexity of the thermal field, introducing multiple competing heat dissipation pathways, in contrast to the more stable thermal trajectories observed in conventional strategies [ 101 ]. Collectively, these effects explain the lower texture intensity observed by EBSD for the 67° condition, demonstrating that this deposition strategy effectively reduces microstructural anisotropy by interrupting epitaxial growth continuity and promoting a more isotropic distribution of crystallographic orientations [ 97 ,  99 ].

Figure  12  presents the inverse pole figure (IPF) maps for each analysis direction, in which the color scale represents the relative intensity of crystallographic orientations with respect to a random distribution. The same color scale was applied to all samples to enable direct comparison. Blocks fabricated with a 67° reorientation angle, regardless of interlayer time, exhibited weaker textures and more homogeneous orientation distributions, whereas those produced with 0° and 90° reorientation angles showed markedly stronger textures, particularly in samples C5-00 and C5-90. Samples C2-00 (AWD), C2-90 (TWD), C5-00 (AWD), and C5-90 (TWD) displayed a predominant [ 99 ]-type texture, encompassing the family of orientations [ 99 ], [010], [001], [ī00], [0ī0], and [00ī], which is indicative of a higher degree of microstructural anisotropy. In contrast, samples C5-00 (BD and AWD) and C5-90 (BD) exhibited pronounced textures associated with [ 100 ], [10ī], and [ī01] orientations. Quantitative analysis of the texture indices reported in Table  6  indicated a differentiated influence of interlayer time depending on the reorientation angle, with a substantial increase of 368.09% for 0° when comparing C5-00 to C2-00, a limited variation of 8.44% for 67°, and an intermediate increase of 124.89% for 90°. These results suggest that crystallographic texture evolution is governed by the combined effect of deposition angle and interlayer time, with direct implications for the development of microstructural anisotropy in the fabricated blocks. Fig. 12 Inverse pole figure (IPF) maps obtained by EBSD, corresponding to each analysis direction and the different manufacturing conditions evaluated Table 6 Microstructural anisotropy indices as a function of manufacturing conditions Sample Minimum index Maximum index C2-00 0.7 2.35 C2-67 0.7 1.54 C2-90 0.7 2.29 C5-00 0.7 11.00 C5-67 0.7 1.67 C5-90 0.7 5.15

Figure  13  presents the main crystallographic orientations and fibers typically observed in steels, which are used as a reference for identifying texture components based on sections of the Orientation Distribution Function (ODF) at φ₂ = 0° and 45°, characteristic of materials with a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure. In samples fabricated with a 0° reorientation angle (C2-00 and C5-00), R-CubeND {001} ⟨110⟩ texture components were predominant, whereas samples produced with a 67° reorientation angle exhibited low orientation intensity, suggesting a reduced degree of overall texturing. For the 90° reorientation angle (C2-90 and C5-90), a predominance of the cube {001} ⟨100⟩ component was observed, with sample C5-90 additionally exhibiting R-GossND {110} ⟨110⟩ and Copper {112} ⟨111⟩ orientations. Texture indices indicated higher intensity for C5-00 (65.68) and C5-90 (42.37), both fabricated with a five-minute interlayer time, whereas the 67° condition generally exhibited the lowest values, with C2-90 showing the minimum index (9.27), close to that of C2-67. Overall, these results suggest that the crystallographic texture depends on the combined effect of the reorientation angle and interlayer time, in agreement with Brito Neto et al. [ 43 ], who reported that a 90° reorientation favors the development of cube, R-CubeRD, and Goss textures in WAAM-fabricated 316L stainless steel. Fig. 13 Orientation Distribution Function (ODF) diagrams at φ2 = 0° and 45° for each condition, and symbolic representation of the main grain orientations and fibers observed in steels

sections.heading: Effect of processing parameters on the tensile mechanical response
paragraphs: Figure  14  presents the mechanical properties obtained along the TWD, AWD, and DD testing directions. ASTM A473 [ 102 ] was considered solely as a comparative benchmark for conventionally forged stainless steels, rather than as a qualification criterion for WAAM components, in order to position the tensile performance of the WAAM-fabricated 316L stainless steel relative to established conventional processing routes. In this context, all samples exceeded the minimum tensile strength requirement specified by ASTM A473 for stainless steels (450 MPa), with no pronounced differences among the evaluated directions, indicating a consistent and predominantly ductile mechanical response. Nevertheless, the mechanical behavior showed sensitivity to the manufacturing parameters, particularly the reorientation angle and the interlayer time. The highest ultimate tensile strength values were associated with the 67° reorientation angle, notably for condition C2-67, which reached 594.44 MPa (TWD), whereas the lowest values were observed under the 0° condition, such as C5-00, with 493.42 MPa (TWD). Regarding yield strength, the maximum value was recorded for C5-67, attaining 328.54 MPa (DD), while the minimum value of approximately 250.31 MPa was observed for C2-00 (AWD). In terms of ductility, the highest elongation values were obtained under the 0° reorientation condition, particularly for C2-00, which exhibited an elongation of 64.28% (AWD), whereas the lowest elongation was recorded for C5-90, at approximately 46.45% (AWD). Fig. 14 Mechanical properties (UTS, YS, and elongation) of WAAM-fabricated samples under different processing conditions and testing directions (TWD, AWD, and DD)

Microstructural analysis was consistent with the mechanical results, highlighting a clear relationship between grain size and mechanical performance. Conditions associated with higher tensile strength, such as C2-67 and C2-90, exhibited more refined microstructures, whereas samples with lower strength, including C2-00 and C5-00, displayed coarser grains, as indicated by the EBSD maps shown in Fig.  11 . Finer microstructures were also associated with reduced elongation, while coarser grains promoted greater deformability, in agreement with established metallurgical principles whereby grain refinement enhances strength by impeding dislocation motion, whereas larger grains facilitate plastic deformation. This behavior is consistent with reports on additively manufactured stainless steels, in which increased strength is commonly attributed to high solidification rates, the formation of dendritic or cellular substructures, and elevated dislocation densities induced by rapid cooling and residual stresses [ 103 ,  104 ,  105 – 106 ]. Conversely, the reduced ductility is generally linked to the inverse relationship between strength and elongation, as well as to dislocation accumulation at grain boundaries or internal defects under tensile loading [ 106 ,  107 ,  108 – 109 ].

Figure  15  synthesizes the mechanical behavior of the material in the TWD, AWD, and DD directions as a function of the reorientation angle and interlayer time, highlighting the combined influence of these parameters on tensile strength, yield strength, and ductility. Regarding ultimate tensile strength (UTS), the TWD direction exhibited values ranging from 493.42 MPa (C5-00) to 594.44 MPa (C2-67), with the highest strengths associated with the 2 min interlayer time, particularly for the 67° configuration. When the interlayer time was increased to 5 min, a general reduction in UTS was observed, although the 90° condition showed the best relative performance within this set. In the AWD direction, UTS displayed lower dispersion, indicating a more reproducible mechanical response, with peak values again concentrated at 67° for both interlayer times (594.44 MPa for C2-67 and 555.80 MPa for C5-67). In contrast, the DD direction showed moderate variations between the 0° and 67° conditions, reaching a maximum in C5-67 (571.74 MPa), while the 90° configuration resulted in a more pronounced strength reduction, particularly in C5-90 (527.62 MPa), corresponding to a decrease of approximately 7.6% relative to C2-90. Collectively, these trends emphasize the central role of the reorientation angle in governing the mechanical response by influencing microstructural development during deposition, in agreement with observations reported by [ 43 ]. Fig. 15 Comparative results of the mechanical properties of the analyzed samples.  a  Ultimate tensile strength, UTS (MPa);  b  Yield strength, YS (MPa); and  c  Elongation (%). The graphs illustrate the variation of these properties in the diagonal (DD), transverse (TWD), and advancing (AWD) directions, highlighting the influence of reorientation angle and interlayer time on the mechanical behavior of the material

Similar tendencies were observed for yield strength (YS), with increased values in the TWD direction for longer interlayer times, especially at 90° (C5-90 = 307.81 MPa), whereas in the AWD and DD directions the highest YS values were again concentrated at 67°, particularly for C5-67, albeit accompanied by increased data scatter attributed to the inherent microstructural heterogeneity of the WAAM process. In terms of ductility, the highest elongation values were associated with the 0° configuration, notably in C2-00, which reached 64.27% in TWD, 53.83% in AWD, and 56.68% in DD. The 67° conditions exhibited intermediate elongation levels with reduced dispersion, whereas the 90° configuration led to more pronounced reductions in elongation, especially for C5-90, indicating a consistent loss of plastic deformation capacity. Despite these directional trends, Tukey statistical analysis at a 95% confidence level did not identify statistically significant differences among the testing directions, suggesting that the observed variations reflect localized microstructural effects rather than pronounced mechanical anisotropy.

This macroscopic behavior can be further contextualized by the work of Gupta and Mulik on WAAM-fabricated Inconel 825, where the selected processing parameters produced comparable tensile responses in the horizontal and vertical directions of the deposited wall, which the authors described as an almost isotropic mechanical behavior. As reported by the authors, the microstructural response included grain refinement and predominantly equiaxed features. Here, the absence of statistically significant differences among TWD, AWD, and DD follows the same general trend, indicating that the tensile response for the 316L stainless steel was not governed by strong directional anisotropy [ 95 ]. This interpretation is supported by EBSD results, which indicated the absence of a dominant crystallographic texture, and is consistent with literature reports stating that mechanical anisotropy in WAAM-fabricated austenitic stainless steels is primarily associated with the development of strong crystallographic textures [ 110 ,  111 ]. Accordingly, the directional tendencies identified here can be linked to columnar dendrite alignment and the multilayer architecture of the deposit, as also reported by Sasikumar et al. [ 112 ], without compromising the achievement of a globally homogeneous mechanical response.

In this context, the absence of statistically significant directional differences does not necessarily contradict the crystallographic texture identified by EBSD but rather suggests that its effect on the macroscopic response was limited. This can be rationalized by considering that crystallographic anisotropy is only clearly manifested as mechanical anisotropy when the texture is sufficiently intense and spatially coherent to dominate the deformed volume. Since EBSD characterizes a specific section of the material, it captures local texture features that may vary spatially and may not fully represent the entire gauge volume subjected to tensile loading [ 74 ,  113 ]. Moreover, in austenitic stainless steels, the γ phase, with its FCC structure and multiple active slip systems, tends to promote a more homogeneous plastic deformation, thereby reducing the sensitivity of the macroscopic response to local crystallographic orientation [ 114 ,  115 ].

This effect may be further reinforced by other microstructural features typical of WAAM, such as grain size, the coexistence of columnar and equiaxed grains, residual ferrite fraction and morphology, solidification substructures, porosity, inclusions, residual stresses, and as-built geometry, since their contribution to mechanical anisotropy depends not only on their presence, but also on their spatial distribution and directional character [ 16 ,  116 ,  117 ,  118 ,  119 – 120 ]. In particular, the fact that the 67° condition combined relatively weaker texture with comparatively high strength suggests that texture intensity alone was not sufficient to explain the observed behavior, and that additional mechanisms, such as microstructural refinement associated with interruption of epitaxial growth, may also have contributed. Thus, the directional tendencies observed here are better interpreted as the result of interacting with local microstructural factors rather than pronounced global mechanical anisotropy.

sections.heading: Corrosion analysis of WAAM-fabricated samples
paragraphs: The potentiodynamic polarization curves obtained for all analyzed samples are presented in Figs.  17 a, enabling a direct comparison of the electrochemical behavior as a function of the manufacturing conditions and testing directions. From these curves, the main electrochemical parameters, including the corrosion potential E corr , the pitting potential E pitting,  and the corrosion current i corr , were determined and are summarized in Table  8 . It is observed that all polarization curves exhibited fluctuations in current density, a phenomenon widely reported in the literature [ 125 ,  126 ,  127 ,  128 – 129 ]. commonly associated with the nucleation and early growth of metastable pits, which induce current variations even at potentials below E pitting . As the test progresses, the repassivation of these metastable sites promotes current stabilization, reflecting a dynamic balance between dissolution and repassivation processes. The magnitude of current fluctuations varied among the samples, indicating the influence of manufacturing conditions on the electrochemical response, which may be associated with microstructural differences affecting the formation and stability of the passive film. Fig. 17 a ,  c  Potentiodynamic polarization curves obtained in 0.6 mol L −1  NaCl solution for WAAM-fabricated samples, and  b ,  d j  (A cm −2 )  versus  E/SCE (V) representation for the E pitting  determination Table 8 Electrochemical parameters of WAAM-fabricated samples obtained under different deposition conditions and analysis directions C2-00 C5-00 TWD AWD B D TWD AWD B D E corr  (V/SCE) 0.150 0.167 0.140 − 0.127 0.136 − 0.080 i corr  (µA cm -2 ) 0.037 0.027 0.026 0.019 0.026 0.016 E pitting  (V/SCE) 0.428 0.385 0.362 0.357 0.410 0.282 C2− 67 C5− 67 TWD AWD B D TWD AWD B D E corr  (V/SCE) − 0.101 − 0.350 − 0.060 − 0.046 − 0.014 − 0.261 i corr  (µA cm -2 ) 0.022 0.035 0.011 0.008 0.038 0.062 E pitting  (V/SCE) 0.356 0.345 0.343 0.391 0.336 0.133 C2− 90 C5− 90 TWD AWD B D TWD AWD B D E corr (V/SCE) 0.163 0.129 0.064 0.012 − 0.201 0.062 i corr  (µA cm -2 ) 0.027 0.033 0.021 0.013 0.041 0.026 E pitting  (V/SCE) 0.383 0.366 0.401 0.401 0.345 0.327

After analysis of the samples and their respective extraction directions, as summarized in Table  8 , the TWD direction generally exhibited a more favorable electrochemical response compared with the other orientations. This behavior is reflected by less negative E corr  values and more positive E pitting  values under specific conditions, indicating a higher tendency toward passivation. The polarization curves presented in Figs.  17 a, b enable a global comparison of the electrochemical behavior of all samples. Although i corr  values were, in some cases, comparable among directions, the TWD orientation showed a more stable response for the C2-00, C5-67, and C5-90 conditions. A more detailed examination of the polarization curves corresponding to the C5-67 TWD and C5-90 TWD conditions, shown in Figs.  17 c, d, reveals a more favorable behavior when compared with C2-00 TWD, which, despite exhibiting a more noble E corr , presented higher i corr  values.

Previous studies have shown that both the deposition strategy and the reorientation angle in WAAM directly influence the corrosion resistance of austenitic stainless steels [ 44 ]. Furthermore, zigzag deposition strategies combined with intermediate to high reorientation angles (e.g., 45° and 90°) yielded less negative E corr , more noble E pitting , and reduced i corr  for parameter combinations.

These findings indicate that appropriate control of WAAM processing parameters can significantly enhance electrochemical performance. This trend is consistent with the results of the present study, in which the conditions employing reorientation angles of 67° and 90° generally exhibited improved corrosion behavior. Evaluation along the three principal analysis directions further revealed slightly superior corrosion resistance in the transverse plane (TWD), in agreement with previous reports attributing corrosion anisotropy in additively manufactured components to differences in solidification rates among build directions [ 130 ]. In this context, Wang et al. [ 76 ] demonstrated that enhanced heat dissipation along the build direction promotes microstructural variations, including changes in dendritic arm spacing and increased segregation of Cr and Mo into the ferritic phase, which favors the formation of galvanic microcells and reduces corrosion resistance [ 131 ]. Conversely, directions associated with higher cooling rates tend to develop more refined microstructures, thereby contributing to improved electrochemical performance. Accordingly, the superior corrosion resistance observed in the TWD plane in the present work is in good agreement with these mechanisms reported in the literature.

Beyond the effects associated with reorientation angle, Wang et al. [ 76 ] emphasized that ferrite content plays a decisive role in the corrosion behavior of austenitic stainless steels, as lower ferrite fractions generally enhance the corrosion resistance of low-Cr austenite [ 132 ,  133 ]. However, segregation of Cr and Mo into the ferritic phase reduces the availability of these elements in the austenitic matrix, thereby compromising the stability of the protective passive film [ 71 ]. In this context, the more favorable electrochemical performance observed in the TWD direction in the present study may be attributed to a lower degree of elemental segregation, a reduced ferrite fraction, and a more refined dendritic microstructure, which is also consistent with the higher ultimate tensile strength (UTS) values obtained for this orientation. As illustrated in Fig.  10 , the fabricated samples exhibited variable fractions of body-centered cubic (BCC) ferrite, depending on the processing conditions employed. Higher ferrite contents tend to intensify galvanic coupling between ferrite and austenite, thereby increasing susceptibility to corrosion. Electrochemical results reported by Wang et al. [ 76 ] corroborate this interpretation, showing higher corrosion potentials in the transverse plane and lower values in the build-direction plane, as well as more active E pitting  values in the advancing and transverse planes, suggesting a predominance of more aggressive pitting mechanisms in these orientations.

Pitting corrosion in austenitic stainless steels is widely associated with the localized dissolution of MnS inclusions, which reduces the Cr:Fe ratio in the surrounding matrix and promotes pit initiation in Cr-depleted regions [ 78 ,  134 ,  135 ]. In WAAM-fabricated 316L steels, such inclusions are typically small, and the transition from metastable to stable pits is governed primarily by the progressive dissolution of these inclusions rather than by direct passive film breakdown [ 136 ,  137 – 138 ]. Previous studies have shown that more active E pitting  values in the transverse and advancing planes are linked to variations in ferrite fraction and phase segregation [ 76 ], with higher ferrite contents shifting E pitting  toward more active potentials and narrowing the passive range [ 139 ,  140 ]. Accordingly, the variations in E pitting  observed in the present study are predominantly attributed to local microstructural features, particularly elemental segregation and ferrite distribution across the different analysis directions. Previous studies indicate that pitting corrosion preferentially initiates at surface regions containing intrinsic defects or deleterious inclusions, such as manganese sulfides and oxides, which compromise the stability of Cr- and Fe-rich passive layers through localized chromium depletion [ 4 ,  10 ,  123 ,  141 ].

In the present study, linear EDS analyses confirmed the predominant presence of oxide inclusions, which may act as preferential anodic sites in chloride-containing environments, thereby facilitating localized corrosion initiation. As corrosion progresses, the accumulation of corrosion products within pit cavities can restrict mass transport and induce temporary repassivation; however, under more aggressive conditions, this process tends to become irreversible, leading to accelerated pit propagation and a significant reduction in material service life. Overall, the results reinforce that the susceptibility of WAAM-fabricated 316L stainless steel to localized corrosion is strongly governed by the presence of inclusions and the microstructure developed during processing, underscoring the importance of precise control of manufacturing parameters to optimize performance in aggressive environments.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The optimization of the WAAM process using 316L stainless steel demonstrated that the appropriate combination of welding speed, wire feed rate, bead spacing, interlayer time, and reorientation angle directly affects process efficiency, geometrical quality, and the functional properties of the fabricated parts; A higher welding speed combined with a smaller bead spacing produced deposits with greater aspect ratio, height, and surface regularity, resulting in improved dimensional stability and lower energy consumption. Conversely, reducing the interlayer time increased productivity by up to 44.4%, but compromised surface uniformity, particularly in samples with 0° reorientation; From a microstructural perspective, EBSD analyses revealed the predominance of austenite (FCC) and a significant reduction of ferrite (BCC) at 67° and 90° reorientation angles, especially under longer interlayer times. These conditions promoted thermal and microstructural stability, minimized anisotropy, and resulted in more isotropic mechanical behavior. Crystallographic texture was also sensitive to reorientation and interlayer time: extreme angles (0° and 90°) led to more intense, anisotropic textures, while 67° produced a more homogeneous grain structure with weaker texture components, such as R-CubeND and Cube, allowing better control of grain orientation according to design requirements; In terms of mechanical performance, samples fabricated with a 67° reorientation angle exhibited the best balance between strength and isotropy, making this configuration suitable for applications requiring directional uniformity. The AWD direction showed good reproducibility, reinforcing its potential for predictable structural applications; The electrochemical behavior was enhanced in samples produced with a 2 min interlayer time and 67° reorientation, particularly in the TWD direction, which exhibited more noble E corr  and superior passive stability. Microstructural variations among build directions accounted for differences in corrosion susceptibility, underscoring the need for precise thermal and geometric control during deposition; Overall, the results confirm that the deposition strategy in WAAM is a key factor in defining the texture, microstructure, mechanical strength, and durability of 316L stainless steel components. Reorientation angle and interlayer time act as strategic tools to tailor performance according to application requirements, enhancing the industrial viability and reliability of WAAM-fabricated metallic parts for demanding sectors requiring high mechanical strength and corrosion resistance.
